newsitem.title: UK: Dutch footballer claimed cash came from car theft.
newsitem.headline: Dutch footballer claimed cash came from car theft.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, on trial for match-fixing, told police the large sums he paid into a Swiss bank account came from car thefts carried out many years ago, a court heard on Wednesday.

But chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith told the jury that the explanation was implausible and said it was likely the money had come from a Far Eastern betting syndicate which paid Dutchman Segers for arranging the results of matches.

Segers and three other defendants are on trial accused of accepting or giving money to rig matches in the first case of its kind in Britain for more than 30 years. All four -- who plead not guilty -- could be jailed for up to seven years.

Asked to explain the large amounts of money he deposited at the Swiss branch of a U.S. bank in London in 1993 and 1994, Segers told police he had been gradually transferring 250,000 pounds ($420,000) from an offshore account in Jersey.
Segers, 35, said he had stopped adding to the account in 1984 when he moved from the Netherlands to join English club Nottingham Forest.
Pressed by the police as to how he could have amassed so much money at such a young age, the Dutch keeper replied:
"It came from things I've done in the past. I was involved in stealing cars, bits and pieces."
Calvert Smith cast doubt on the story, saying police had found no evidence of a bank account in Jersey. Segers told them he could not remember what the bank had been called.
"The cash payments Segers made into the account were made during the soccer season, and particularly after matches which Wimbledon had lost," the chief prosecutor said.
"His account of the case is far-fetched and not supported by any documents found in his house or any interviews."

Segers told police his partner in crime was dead and also said he had few contacts with fellow defendant John Fashanu and did not know Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim. Both men are accused of acting as middle men for the betting syndicate.
But Calvert Smith said detailed telephone logs showed Segers was lying, since it was clear that he had been in frequent contact with both Lim and Fashanu.
He was particularly dismissive of Segers' assertion that he had no idea who could have been responsible for the many phone calls logged from his various phones to Lim.
"Members of the jury, you may find that hard to believe. We suggest it was an outright lie," said Calvert Smith.
The fourth defendant is former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, accused of taking part in a separate match-rigging conspiracy with Lim and Fashanu.
